newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Information revolution seen critical to growth.
newsitem.headline: Information revolution seen critical to growth.

text.p: The information technology revolution is critical to world growth and countries risk being left behind economically if they do not take part in it, industry and political leaders said on Monday.
Singapore Communications Minister Mah Bow Tan said the information revolution could widen the gap between rich and poor countries.

"The development gap...could worsen if due account is not paid to the specific needs of developing countries and their place in the new information society," he told delegates at the Asia Telecoms 97 trade fair.
"One of the challenges ahead is to cultivate a generation of people who are comfortable with information technology, to fully exploit the potential of IT for a better quality of life," Mah said.
Industry leaders said at the start of the week-long exhibition that bringing the information age within the reach of the world's poorest people was the key to sustainable economic development.

"There has been a recognition at the highest levels of government and industry that universal access to basic communications and information services will be the key to sustainable global development in the 21st Century," said International Telecommunication Union (ITU) secretary general Pekka Tarjanne,

"I think it is fair to say there has been a revolution, not only in the world of telecommunications, but even more importantly, in how the world sees telecommunications," he told delegates from 476 companies and 31 countries.

Telecommunications has become one of the main dynamics driving the economies of Asia as the industry has begun to make the transition from public utility to commercial nervice centre and will become more powerful in future, Tarjanne said.
"Communications and information technology will be the foundation of economic wealth and social progress in the 21st century," Tarjanne said.
Singapore Prime Minister Goh Chok Tong said the information revolution of the 21st century would have greater implications for global trade than the Industrial Revolution.
"The advancements which collectively usher in the Information Era will have a greater impact on our lives than the industrial and technological revolutions before it," Goh said.
"We must make the effort to harness the new communications technologies to make life better and more meantingful for our peoples, whether we are a developed or developing country," he said.

The social responsibility of telecommunications companies has emerged as a key theme of thE four-yearly gathering and is particularly relevant in Asia, where two-thirds of the population does not have access to even the most basic of telephone services.
"The teledensity of the emerging economies is still well below other regions of the world, such as the Middle East," Tarjanne said.

"The telecommunications industry has the capital to contribute to making the world a bit of a better place," said Christopher B. Galvin, chief executive officer of global communications giant Motorola Inc.
Galvin said rapid advances in telecommunications technology must be quickly turned into "products and services that improve the way people live".
